composed by Padmavajra;
Sarnath edition.
Ka = CIHTS microfilm no. 21548, fols. 6–17, Newari;

[211] Now, the two aspects—wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*)—are examined. What is called wisdom? It is characterized by non-deviation from the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation. Wisdom is twofold: analytical (*pratyavekṣaṇā*) and penetrative (*nairvedhikī*). That which examines, investigates, and knows each thing individually, and is grasped by the vajra-eye, is analytical wisdom. Penetrative wisdom is that by which one penetrates through that very analysis; it is penetrative wisdom.

That penetrative wisdom (*nairvedhikī prajñā*)—which will be explained clearly later—renders all things, such as self, sentient beings, and life-force, as devoid of self through the intellect; it brings about direct realization and becomes exceedingly difficult to conquer, meaning it becomes invincible.
Furthermore, the fourfold means (*upāya*) has been described by Bodhivajra—that is, by Buddhavajra. First is the ritual of service (*sevā*), and second is the near-attainment (*upasādhana*).
The third is the *sādhana* and the fourth is the *mahāsādhana*.
Furthermore, this is as follows: the first is the realization of emptiness (*śūnyatābodhi*), and the second is the withdrawal into the vajra (*vajrasaṃhṛti*).
The third is the completion of the image, and the fourth is the other, the syllable.
By these four vajras, the perfection of gnosis is described.

212] For this very reason, wisdom has the characteristic of non-existence, while means has the characteristic of existence. And so it has been said: "Wisdom has the characteristic of being without intrinsic nature, and means has the characteristic of intrinsic nature."
Therefore, by means of that [dharma], the practitioner's cyclic existence increases;
the five strands of sensual pleasure are considered to be the affliction of fools. || 3 ||
Furthermore, by means of that very dharma, the yogin should accomplish Buddhahood:
passion, exhilaration, joy, as well as loving-kindness and compassion. (4)
Equanimity and joy, as well as strength and enthusiasm;
likewise heroism, vigor, ferocity, obstinacy, and recklessness—these are the other natures whose essential forms he should traverse by means of self-mastery. (5)
Either joined with a single mudrā or endowed with four mudrās,
or even while within the inner apartments, one should practice the recollection of self-consecration.
Established in the state of great bliss, the yogi should always experience beautiful forms, sounds, likewise smells, tastes, and tactile sensations. (7)

Then, by means of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*), the yogi should enter into these four kinds of musical instruments: the covered (*āvanaddha*), the gong (*ghaṭa*), and the wind instrument (*śuṣira*). (8)

Through the samādhi that is like an illusion, the yogi should always experience all the aesthetic sentiments (rasas), beginning with the erotic, which are designated as the nine dramatic modes (nāṭya).
Whatever extensive stobhas and so forth are taught in the Yoga Tantras, the yogin should employ them through illusion, by way of non-apprehension. 10.
Whether opening or closing his eyes, laughing or speaking, walking, standing, sleeping, or eating, he should constantly recollect the illusory body (māyādeha). || 11 ||
Furthermore, whatever other games exist in the world, fashioned by various conceptualizations,
the knower of reality should engage in them while remaining established in the system of Great Passion.
Having attained this self-consecration, which shatters all views, one may do everything or do nothing at all, acting according to one's own inclination. (13)
One should not perform rites for a shrine, nor recite from a book;
however, one may indeed perform or cause [others] to recite according to the sequence of self-consecration.
One should not salute the gods in this manner, nor should one salute the monks;
or else, one may salute all of them according to the sequence of self-consecration.
One should not perform the ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*), nor likewise the binding of mudrās;
one should not perform the recitation of mantras (*mantrajāpa*), or if one does, it should be like a reflection.
My own mind is what is seen; external objects do not exist. One should indeed contemplate phenomena in this way and likewise recollect suchness. (17)
If Māyā were not attained through the method of infinite meditation and the meditative absorption on the mantra-form, then the entire ground would indeed bear fruit.
The body, enjoyments, and the environment, as well as the stages, the perfections, and so forth, and all the miraculous transformations of a Buddha—all these are the play of illusion. (19)
Just as a complete form, perfectly joined and exceedingly clear, shines within the mirror-image,
so too [does he] endowed with the eighty secondary marks and the primary marks.
The body is likewise always Vajradhara. || 20 ||

"The rainbow seen in the sky displays its many colors as a sign of the world's auspicious and inauspicious karma. Differentiated by the application of the instruments, they then perform the welfare of sentient beings, just like a multiform jewel. Thus it is said.
Thus far, it has been established that there are two parts: wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*).

Now, this is explained: could Buddhahood be attained by wisdom alone? Or [could it be attained] by skillful means alone? To this it is said: Buddhahood does not arise through wisdom alone, nor does it arise through skillful means alone; rather, if wisdom and skillful means possess the characteristic of equality and are of the nature of sameness, such that these two become non-dual in form, then there is both enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*).
And so it has been said:
Because it brings about the desired object, like a boat being steered with a favorable current,
that very [method] is proclaimed as the "means" (upāya) through its application of favorability.
And that which is the merging of both, like water and milk,
through the application of a non-dual form— that is called wisdom and means (prajñopāya).
That in which neither addition nor subtraction can be made,
and wherein both wisdom and skillful means have been relinquished— that is called the true nature of phenomena (dharmatattva).
Like a wish-fulfilling gem, he remains forever for the entire world as the perfect state of enjoyment and liberation, by virtue of his nature as wisdom and skillful means.

"Having realized this very [reality], the perfectly awakened Sugatas of the past attained enlightenment, they are attaining enlightenment everywhere, and those who work for the welfare of the world will attain enlightenment," thus [it is said]. (Pra. Vi. Si. 1.16–18, 25–26)

If, however, one were to make a division into two parts, thinking "this is wisdom" and "this is method," then Buddhahood would not occur. But if, through the single-formed nature of these two as emptiness, a consciousness arises that reaches the ultimate limit of perfect excellence, then it is certain that for yogins, Buddhahood and the state of Vajradhara will be attained in this very life. Furthermore, such knowledge does not arise devoid of wisdom and method.

Knowledge consisting of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*) arises. What need is there for much more? Through the thorough understanding of the two—wisdom and means—liberation is attained by yogins. Therefore, all beings within the three realms and so forth have as their nature that which is produced from wisdom and means. For this very reason, the Buddha, the Blessed One, by the power of his great compassion and aspirational prayers, manifests the dharma of liberation as a single-form knowledge for each [being], appearing in whatever diverse forms they may have through the yoga of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) and the twofold distinction between knowledge and the object of knowledge.
Therefore, having heard that all phenomena are primordially pure and naturally luminous, this was said by the Blessed Buddha: as it is stated in the tantra known as the *Saṃvara*:
"These very Perfect Buddhas arise from a single cause."

"Furthermore, they are born again in previous eons due to the causes of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) and afflictions (*kleśa*). Therefore, for that reason... [all] sentient beings are embraced because of the excellence of love for many sons toward the Truth. And so it has been said: "Who told us that the Buddha, the Blessed One, has awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment? As long as we have not established all sentient beings of the three realms in Buddhahood, we do not receive the name "Buddha. And so it is said in the *Bhadracaryāpraṇidhāna*:
"As long as there is no end to those beings, and likewise no end to sentient beings without exception;
as far as there is an end to karma and afflictions, so far shall be the end of my vow.
And so it is said in the *Samādhirāja Sūtra*:
"All these people shall become Buddhas; indeed, there is no sentient being who is not a fit vessel. (Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra, Chapter on the Analysis of the Vowels, Verse 72, p. 317)

Therefore, for this purpose, the Blessed One, whose form is the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, by the power of his great compassion and vows, remains established as the duality of wisdom and means. Abiding in the forms of the Dharma-body, Enjoyment-body, and Emanation-body, and in the forms with and without aspects, he manifests a diverse drama of wisdom and means for the sake of fortunate sentient beings. Through the thorough understanding of this drama of wisdom and means, one attains Buddhahood and the state of Vajradhara even in this very life.

Herein, the instruction is joined together. What is called "wisdom" (prajñā)? Wisdom is designated as the lotus. In the word "wisdom," there is a doubt; therefore, by way of the nature of the lotus, wisdom is said to be by its very nature the five goddesses—Locanā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍarā, Tārā, and Samantabhadrā—whose nature is emptiness (śūnyatā). That is to say, the five elements, such as earth, water, fire, air, and space, are established in the form of emptiness.

Thus, by means of that very nature of emptiness, the five deities—Locanā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍaravāsinī, Tārā, and Samantabhadra—are transformed therein. Furthermore, the deities Akṣobhya, Ratnasaṃbhava, Amitābha, Amoghasiddhi, Śrī-Vairocana, and the others, through the yoga of the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya), assume a glorious form and are transformed into the forms of the five goddesses beginning with Locanā.

The deity Samantabhadrā, whose essence is the nature of emptiness, is Prajñāpāramitā; she exists as the four goddesses whose nature is gnosis, established through the process of emanation and reabsorption. Samantabhadrā, whose essential nature is the transformation of the gnosis of the form of Śrī Mahāvairocana, is designated by the term "Prajñāpāramitā."

In brief, that Prajñāpāramitā which is Samantabhadrā is of the nature of non-existence; by virtue of having the characteristic of space, it has the aspect of emptiness, is secluded, naturally luminous, devoid of both knowledge and the object of knowledge, and characterized by the absence of intrinsic nature. Being transformed as the Dharmakāya, she manifests as the Saṃbhogakāya for those to be trained, and through that, appears as the Nirmāṇakāya and so forth. Furthermore, even the Saṃbhogakāya has the characteristic of emptiness.

And emptiness is established as being endowed with the excellence of all aspects; it is realized as having a nature that is like an illusion, a mirage, a dream, a reflection, an echo, the moon in water, and a magical creation. Thus it has been said: "Having made the enjoyment body (sāmbhogikakāya) empty, the Dharma body and the emanation body (nairmāṇikakāya) were taught by all the Buddhas."

What is expressed by the term *prajñopāya* (wisdom-means)? It means "means through wisdom" (*prajñayā upāyaḥ*), that is to say, means generated by wisdom. What meaning is denoted by this word "means"? The glorious Vajrasattva, who is the nature of compassion, who has become the world (*saṃsāra*), and whose form is the essence of the stable reality—this is what is called by the word "means. Thus, "means" is the glorious Vajrasattva. He is established as having the nature of emanation and reabsorption, consisting of the five bodies (*pañcakāya*) and the five Tathāgatas.
[p. 217] By the union of the vajra and the lotus...

One should meditate on the nature of gnosis (jñāna) in a single form embraced by wisdom (prajñā). What is the relationship between these two, wisdom and means (upāya)? The five deities, Locanā and the others, are transformed into the form of emptiness (śūnyatā) through their nature as the elements and so forth. Means (upāya), moreover, is the glorious Vajrasattva, whose nature is all phenomena; that which is the emptiness of the nature of all stable and moving phenomena is transformed through the yoga of the form of emptiness. By these two syllables, "Oṃ Hūṃ," there is a single form.

For the purpose of establishing wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*), he has assumed a twofold form; yet Vajrasattva does not undergo a state of duality. When that which is empty is pervaded by emptiness, then it appears as a single form. Furthermore, all sentient beings consist of wisdom and skillful means; therefore, for those who create a division between the natures of wisdom and skillful means, they remain fallen on the other side after having playfully beheld the *saṃbhoga* [kāya], seized by the grasp of ignorance (*vidyā*).

Furthermore, those who perceive and cultivate the non-dual form as the nature of reality by way of its pure aspect are attainers of the fruit of unsurpassed enlightenment. Therefore, because they possess the dual nature of both wisdom and skillful means, there is no bondage whatsoever for the Blessed Buddhas. A certain wise person becomes liberated through the yoga of equanimity. And so it has been said: "By that which fools are bound, by that the awakened are released;
through the cultivation of awakening, all this [duality] is reversed."
And it is further said:

"By whatever state of being one applies oneself here and there through the power of habituation, one manifests a more distinguished nature characterized by the quality of not seeing [existence] again. And thus it has been said:
"By whatever state of being the minds of men are joined..."
Through that, one attains identity with it, just as a gem assumes the form of everything reflected within it.
And it is further said:
"By whatever fierce karma sentient beings are bound, by that very same means, through skillful methods, they are liberated from the bonds of existence. (Hevajra Tantra 2.2.50)
And so it has been said:
"Those who are overwhelmed by desire, grief, fear, madness, thieves, dreams, and the like,"
They see even non-existent things as if they were standing right before them.
Therefore, whether it be real or unreal, whatever is meditated upon,
when the power of that meditation reaches completion, the result is a cognition of that object in its totality.
One who is attached even to compassion and the like, though they may be subtle, does not attain the supreme path.
Alternatively, if one cultivates compassion [toward worldly beings], that person does not attain liberation from saṃsāra.
Furthermore, he who is praised cannot be separated from this;
he remains neither in worldly existence nor in nirvāṇa.

This is the meaning: regarding the term "compassion" (*karuṇā*). If one devoid of compassion engages with emptiness (*śūnyatā*), then that yogi does not attain the supreme path; that is to say, he does not attain the path to Buddhahood. Alternatively, if one devoid of emptiness cultivates compassion alone, then liberation from cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is not attained. However, the yogi who, having understood these two aspects, is able to join the two masses of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*), and is able to make them of a single form—for him there is neither existence nor nirvāṇa; here "existence" refers to cyclic existence and "nirvāṇa" refers to Buddhahood.
That divine [syllable] in the shape of the letter *E*, adorned in its center with the syllable *Vaṃ*, is the abode of all Buddhas and the jewel-casket of the Buddha.
The letter *E* is said to be the lotus; they call the letter *Vaṃ* the vajra.
There the Buddhas have arisen; there indeed they have entered final nirvāṇa. Thus ends the *Advayavivaraṇaprajñopāyaviniścayasiddhi*.
This is the work of the venerable master Padmavajra.
